title: Gospel of Mark
intro: 40 days through the Gospel of Mark, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: Mark's first line works like a title for the whole book. It calls the story "good news," the meaning of "gospel," and names Jesus with the two titles Mark sets out to show are true: Christ, the promised Messiah, and Son of God. Mark is the shortest of the four Gospels, and many scholars think it was the first written, around 65 to 70 AD. Starting today, 40 days through Mark, one verse at a time.

As Jesus comes up out of the Jordan River after John baptizes him, Mark describes the Spirit coming down like a dove and a voice from heaven speaking to him. The point is God's own verdict on Jesus before he has preached or healed anyone: he is God's beloved Son, and God delights in him. The words echo Psalm 2, about God's anointed king, and Isaiah 42, about God's chosen servant.

After John the Baptist is arrested, Jesus goes into Galilee, and these are his first words in Mark, a summary of his whole message. The point is that the long wait is over: God's kingdom is arriving, so people should turn their lives around and trust the good news. "Repent" translates the Greek verb metanoeo, literally a change of mind or direction, not just feeling sorry.

Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus sees two brothers, Simon (later called Peter) and Andrew, casting their nets. He calls them to follow him and turns their own trade into a picture of their new work: gathering people instead of fish. Mark says they left their nets at once. Jesus' first followers were ordinary working people, called just as they were.

The evening before, the whole town of Capernaum had gathered at the door of the house where Jesus was staying, bringing their sick to be healed. Now he gets up before dawn to be alone and pray. Mark shows this pattern more than once: busy public days balanced with quiet time away.

Four friends can't get through the crowd, so they dig through the roof and lower their paralyzed friend down to Jesus. Jesus responds to their faith, and he starts with forgiveness rather than healing. That is the heart of the story: the religious teachers watching are shocked, since they believe only God can forgive sins, and Jesus then heals the man to show he has that authority.

Jesus has called Levi, a tax collector, to follow him, and is now eating at Levi's house with tax collectors and "sinners," people treated as outsiders. Tax collectors worked for Rome and were often seen as traitors and cheats. When critics object, Jesus answers with an analogy: a doctor goes where the sick are. His point is that he came for the very people others had written off.

posts.display: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.”
posts.caption: The Sabbath is the weekly day of rest from the Ten Commandments. Jesus' disciples were criticized for picking grain to eat on it. His point: the day of rest was given as a gift to serve people, not as a burden people exist to serve.

Some critics claim Jesus drives out demons by the power of Satan. He answers with logic: a house fighting against itself would collapse, so the accusation makes no sense. Abraham Lincoln borrowed this line for his famous 1858 "House Divided" speech about slavery.

The end of the Parable of the Sower. A farmer scatters seed that lands on a path, on rocky ground, among thorns, and on good soil. Jesus explains that the soils are different ways people receive his message, and only the good soil produces a lasting crop. A hundredfold harvest would have sounded almost impossible to a farmer.

posts.display: “To what can we compare the kingdom of God? With what parable shall we present it? It is like a mustard seed, which is the smallest of all seeds sown upon the earth. But after it is planted, it grows to be the largest of all garden plants.”
posts.caption: Jesus compares the kingdom of God to a mustard seed, proverbial for being tiny. The image is about small, unimpressive beginnings that grow far beyond what anyone would expect. He adds that the plant puts out branches big enough for birds to nest in its shade, which many scholars hear as an echo of great trees standing for kingdoms in Ezekiel and Daniel.

A storm hits the disciples' boat on the Sea of Galilee while Jesus sleeps. Several of them were experienced fishermen, and they are terrified. In the Hebrew scriptures, calming the sea is something only God does (see Psalm 107), which is why the question the disciples ask afterward matters so much.

Jesus has just woken in a storm on the Sea of Galilee and ordered the wind and waves to be still, and they obeyed. Now the disciples are more frightened than they were during the storm. Their question is the point: in the Hebrew scriptures, ruling the sea belongs to God, so who is this man? It runs through the first half of Mark and is answered in chapter 8.

A woman who had been bleeding for twelve years touches Jesus' cloak in a crowd, hoping to be healed without anyone noticing. Under the purity customs of the time, her condition would have kept her isolated. Jesus stops, finds her, and calls her "Daughter," restoring her in public as well as in body.

Jairus, a synagogue leader, had begged Jesus to heal his dying daughter. On the way, messengers arrive to say she has died, so why bother the teacher any further? Jesus overhears and tells Jairus not to give in to fear but to keep trusting, even when hope seems gone. The story ends with Jesus raising the girl back to life.

Jesus returns to his hometown of Nazareth and teaches in the synagogue, but the people who watched him grow up can't accept him. "Isn't this the carpenter?" they ask. His reply, probably a familiar proverb, makes the point: those closest to a messenger often find it hardest to hear him. Mark notes that he did few miracles there and was amazed at their unbelief.

The disciples have just returned from their first mission, so busy they haven't even had time to eat. Jesus invites them to get away and rest. Even with crowds waiting, rest is something he makes room for.

Jesus and his disciples try to slip away by boat for some rest, but the crowds run ahead on foot and get there first. Jesus responds with compassion instead of frustration. "Sheep without a shepherd" is an image from the Hebrew scriptures for people without good leaders. What comes next is the feeding of the five thousand.

Religious leaders criticize the disciples for eating without ritual handwashing. Jesus moves the focus from outward rules to the heart. A few verses later he explains what he means: things like greed, deceit, envy, and arrogance are what truly make a person unclean.

The turning point of Mark. After all the "Who is this?" moments, Jesus asks his disciples directly. Peter's answer, "the Christ," is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew word Messiah, meaning "anointed one": the promised king Israel had been waiting for.

Right after Peter calls him the Christ, Jesus tells his disciples he will suffer and die, and Peter objects. Then Jesus says this to everyone: following him means putting self-interest aside, even to the point of losing one's life. In the Roman world, crucifixion was a public execution, and the condemned were made to carry their own cross to it. It was a shocking image, not a decorative one.

Jesus has just told the crowd that following him means taking up a cross. Here he asks a blunt question: what good is winning everything the world offers if it costs you your very self? The Greek word translated "soul," psyche, can also mean "life," and it's the same word as in the verse before: "whoever loses his life for My sake and for the gospel will save it."

A father brings his son, who suffers violent seizures, to Jesus for help. When Jesus tells him that everything is possible for someone who believes, the father answers with this honest admission. Many readers find this verse comforting because it shows belief and doubt existing in the same person.
On the road, the disciples had been arguing about which of them was the greatest. Jesus sits them down and flips their idea of status: in his view, greatness comes through serving others.

People bring their children for Jesus to bless, and the disciples try to send them away. Children had little social status then, but Jesus is indignant, a strong word, and says God's kingdom belongs to people like them. The next verse adds that it must be received like a child, which many readers take to mean with trust, as a gift rather than an achievement. Then he takes them in his arms and blesses them.

A rich man asks Jesus how to inherit eternal life. Jesus tells him to sell what he owns and give to the poor, and the man walks away sad. Jesus then makes the point with deliberate exaggeration: wealth can grip people so tightly that entering God's kingdom becomes humanly impossible. The disciples are stunned, because wealth was often seen as a sign of God's favor.

Jesus has just said it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. Astonished, the disciples ask, "Who then can be saved?" This is his answer: salvation is not something people can achieve on their own, but God can do what people can't.

James and John ask for the seats of honor next to Jesus. He answers that his followers should serve, just as he came to serve. A "ransom" was a price paid to free a captive or a slave. Many readers see this as the key verse explaining why, in Mark's telling, Jesus goes to his death.

During Jesus' last week in Jerusalem, Peter notices that a fig tree Jesus cursed has withered, and Jesus uses it to teach about faith and prayer. He ends with this: prayer and forgiveness go together, so before asking God for anything, let go of what you hold against others. The same link between being forgiven and forgiving appears in the Lord's Prayer in Matthew and Luke.

Opponents try to trap Jesus: should Jews pay taxes to Rome? Saying yes would anger the crowd, and saying no would sound like rebellion. He asks for a coin, points to Caesar's image on it, and gives this answer. Many readers hear an unspoken second half: if the coin bears Caesar's image, people bear God's image (Genesis 1:27).

posts.display: “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’ The second is this: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ No other commandment is greater than these.”
posts.caption: A teacher of the law asks Jesus which commandment is the most important. Jesus answers by quoting two passages from the Torah, Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18. Putting love of God and love of neighbor together as the summary of everything became central to Christian teaching.

Jesus watches people put money into the temple treasury. The rich give large amounts, and a poor widow gives two small copper coins, worth almost nothing. Jesus measures the gift by what it cost her, not by its size.

Chapter 13 is Jesus' long talk to four disciples on the Mount of Olives about the coming destruction of the temple in Jerusalem and the end of the age. (Rome destroyed the temple in 70 AD.) He closes with this contrast: even heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will last. It's a bold claim, since Isaiah 40:8 says the same of God's word.

The Last Supper: a Passover meal Jesus shares with his disciples the night before he dies. Passover remembers Israel's escape from slavery in Egypt. Jesus takes the bread and calls it his body, which is about to be given up in death. His words over the bread, and then the cup, are the origin of the meal Christians still share, known in different churches as Communion, the Eucharist, or the Lord's Supper.

Jesus prays in the garden of Gethsemane, deeply distressed, knowing what is coming. "Abba" is the Aramaic word for father, a close family word. The "cup" is an image for suffering. He asks to be spared, then surrenders to God's will.

In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus asks Peter, James and John to keep watch while he prays, and comes back to find them asleep. This is his warning: stay alert and pray, because good intentions alone give way under pressure. Within hours, all the disciples flee. "The spirit is willing but the flesh is weak" became a common English saying because of this verse.

These are Jesus' last words in Mark. He has hung on the cross since morning, and darkness has covered the land since noon. Around 3 in the afternoon he cries out, in Aramaic, the first line of Psalm 22. Mark doesn't soften the moment: it is a cry of abandonment. Yet the psalm he quotes opens in anguish and ends in trust, and many readers hear that hope in it too.

A Roman centurion, an army officer over roughly 80 soldiers, watches Jesus die. Until now in Mark, only God's voice from heaven and the evil spirits Jesus drove out have called him God's Son. This Roman is the first human to say it, which brings the story full circle back to the very first verse of the book.

Early Sunday morning, women who had followed Jesus come to the tomb to anoint his body with spices. The stone has been rolled away, and a young man dressed in white tells them the news. The point is in his words: the same Jesus who was crucified has risen. Christians read this as God's answer to the cross, and the resurrection is the foundation of their faith.

The risen Jesus sends his eleven remaining disciples to take the good news, the "gospel" of Mark's very first line, to the whole world. These words come from Mark's longer ending (16:9 to 20). The oldest surviving manuscripts stop at verse 8, with the women fleeing the empty tomb in fear, so most scholars think these verses were added later; many churches still read them as Scripture. That's the whole Gospel of Mark. Thank you for reading it with me.
